definition: The process of using a trained model to generate predictions or outputs on new input data, as opposed to training the model.
details: Inference is where most of an LLM's real-world compute cost accumulates over time (since a model may be trained once but run millions of times), driving significant engineering effort toward inference optimization.

explainer.lead: Inference is running a trained model on new inputs to produce outputs, as opposed to training it. It matters because a model is trained once but run millions of times, so inference dominates an LLM's real-world compute cost over time.

tiers.eli5: Training is studying for the exam; inference is actually answering the questions on the day.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers invest heavily in inference optimization — batching, quantization, faster runtimes — since most operating cost lands here. The pitfall is that optimizations improving throughput can degrade output quality or latency.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined as using a trained model to generate predictions or outputs on new input data, distinct from the training process. Because serving repeats far more often than training, cumulative inference compute can exceed training cost.

explainer.example: A translation model trained once is served to thousands of users per minute; the serving — not the training — accounts for most of its lifetime compute.
